subject: Help to code zero altered gamma glmm

messages.author: 2e15ea020b95d9ad
messages.subject: Help to code zero altered gamma glmm
parts:
Hi all,

I am trying to code zero altered gamma glmm (with random intercept in continuous part) using rstan in a way that later would allow to include covariates into binary part of the model. But when I tested the code on simulated data, I could not recover the intercepts, as well as the shape parameter of the gamma distribution. 

Could anyone help me to find out what was wrong? I have several questions (the code file is attached for convenience)

- Why the intercept of the binary part has wrong sign? Maybe I messed up zeros and ones in bernoulli part?
- Is there a way to constrain scale parameter to get rid of a few numerical problems? And is it worth to do, if there are 1-13 such errors?
- Was the random effect coded in the right way in the transformed parameters section? 
- How to choose prior for shape parameter of gamma distribution?

Here is the simulated dataset:

set.seed(123)
N <- 1000           # Sample size
N_re <- 10          # N of groups
n_in_gr <- N/N_re

# Covariate
X1 <- runif(N, -1, 1)

# Random effects
Groups <- rep(1:N_re, each = n_in_gr)
a <- rnorm(N_re, mean = 0, sd = 0.5)

# Binary part
g1  <- 1           # Intercept
eta_bin <- g1      # Intercept only model, just for start
Pi <- exp(eta_bin) / (1 + exp(eta_bin))
W <- rbinom(N, size = 1, prob = Pi)

# Gamma part
b1 <- 1            # Intercept
b2 <- 2            # Slope
eta_cont <- b1 + b2 * X1 + a[Groups]
shape <- 10
Yg <- rgamma(n = N, shape = shape, rate = shape/exp(eta_cont))

# ZI data
Y <- W * Yg

# Data
dat <- data.frame(
  Y = Y,           # ZAG data
  X1 = X1,         # Covariate
  Groups = Groups) # Random factor

This is the modelling code:

library(rstan)

X_cont <- model.matrix(~ X1, data = dat)
X_bin <- model.matrix(~ 1, data = dat)

dM1 <- list(
  N = nrow(dat),        # total number of observations
  Y = dat$Y,            # response variable
  K_bin = ncol(X_bin),  # population-level effects for binary part
  K_cont = ncol(X_cont),# population-level effects for continuous part
  X_bin = X_bin,   # model matrix for binary part
  X_cont = X_cont, # model matrix for continuous part
  N_re = N_re,     # number of random effects
  Groups = Groups) # random factor

cM1 <- "
data {
  int<lower=1> N;      // total number of observations
  vector[N] Y;         // response variable
  int<lower=1> K_bin;  // population-level effects for binary part
  int<lower=1> K_cont; // population-level effects for continuous part
  matrix[N, K_bin]  X_bin; // model matrix for binary part
  matrix[N, K_cont] X_cont;// model matrix for continuous part
  int N_re; // number of random effects
  int<lower=1,upper=N_re> Groups[N]; // map observations to groups
}
parameters {
  vector[K_bin] g;     // effects for binary part
  vector[K_cont] b;    // effects for continuous part
  real a[N_re];        // random effect
  real<lower=0> sigma; // standard deviation of random effect
  real<lower=0.001, upper = 100> shape;  // shape of gamma
}
transformed parameters {
  vector[N] eta_cont;
  vector[N] eta_bin;
  vector[N] A;
  for(n in 1:N){
    A[n] = a[Groups[n]];
  }
    eta_bin = X_bin * g;
    eta_cont = X_cont * b + A;
}
model {
  // prior specifications
  // for intercepts
  b[1] ~ cauchy(0, 10);
  g[1] ~ cauchy(0, 10);
  // for other coefs
  for(i in 2:K_cont){
    b ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
  }
  if (K_bin > 1) {
      for(i in 2:K_bin){
      g ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
    }
  }
  // for random effects
  sigma ~ cauchy(0, 25);
  a ~ normal(0, sigma);
  // for gamma params
  shape ~ gamma(0.01, 0.01);
  // likelihood contribution
  for (n in 1:N) {
    if ( Y[n] == 0 )
      1 ~ bernoulli_logit(eta_bin[n]);
    else
      0 ~ bernoulli_logit(eta_bin[n]);
      Y[n] ~ gamma(shape, shape / exp(eta_cont[n]));
  }
}
"

sM1 <- stan(model_code = cM1, model_name="ZAG",
            data = dM1, seed = 9846,
            iter = 500, chains = 2, cores = 2)

print(sM1, pars = c("b[1]","b[2]","g[1]","sigma", "shape"),
      probs = c(0.025, 0.50, 0.975), digits_summary = 2)

And here are the estimates:

Inference for Stan model: ZAG.
2 chains, each with iter=500; warmup=250; thin=1; 
post-warmup draws per chain=250, total post-warmup draws=500.

       mean se_mean   sd  2.5%   50%  97.5% n_eff Rhat
b[1]   0.46    0.02 0.17  0.11  0.46   0.77    56 1.02
b[2]   1.95    0.00 0.01  1.94  1.95   1.96   353 1.00
g[1]  -1.03    0.00 0.07 -1.17 -1.03  -0.89   214 1.00
sigma  0.63    0.02 0.19  0.39  0.59   1.16   116 1.01
shape 99.99    0.00 0.01 99.95 99.99 100.00   186 1.01

Samples were drawn using NUTS(diag_e) at Fri Dec 23 10:00:03 2016.
For each parameter, n_eff is a crude measure of effective sample size,
and Rhat is the potential scale reduction factor on split chains (at 
convergence, Rhat=1).

Thank you in advance for your help,

Marina

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Help to code zero altered gamma glmm
parts:
There may be other issues, but if you want to implement a zero-inflation model then
you need to implement a _mixture_ between the mass at zero and the rest of your
distribution. See the "Zero-Inflated and Hurdle Models” section of the manual. That
said, when you mix a discrete and continuous distribution you have to be careful to
not evaluate the continuous density at bad points.

But I may be misunderstanding the model that you’re trying to build — it’ll probably
be easiest if you can write out the model you’re trying to implement in math.

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Help to code zero altered gamma glmm
parts:
I see. Technically the implementation of the Hurdle Model example is correct
but I would not recommend it given that obfuscates the meaning of the model
and requires some potentially unstable intermediate calculations. I recommend
implementing the mixture directly, a la

if (y[n] == 0)
target += log_inv_logit( X_bin[n] * g);
else
target += log1m_inv_logit(X_bin[n] * g) + gamma_lpdf(y[n] | alpha, beta);

Also, you’ll want an intercept when modeling the logit probability.

But that shouldn’t affect your results all that much. Instead you have some
problems with your prior specifications that are the more likely culprit.
> real<lower=0.001, upper = 100> shape; // shape of gamma

> …
> shape ~ gamma(0.01, 0.01);

Bad news. See our recommendations in https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Prior-Choice-Recommendations.

> for(i in 2:K_cont){
> b ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
> }
> if (K_bin > 1) {
> for(i in 2:K_bin){
> g ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
> }
> }

You’re missing the index on the b and g here! Because of the implicit vectorization
you’re actually applying priors to all of the elements of b and g multiple times,
definitely skewing the results. Either add a “[i]” to the above code or you can do
some cute vector manipulations, such as

tail(b, K_cont - 1) ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);

This will give a warning about Jacobians which you can safely ignore.

> a ~ normal(0, sigma);

You’ll probably want to try a non-centered parameterization for the random effects.
See the manual for details.

messages.author: 2e15ea020b95d9ad
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Help to code zero altered gamma glmm
parts:
Thank you a lot for your advice, Michael!

As you suggested, I explicitly coded the mixture of two distributions, and changed the prior of the shape parameter

Thank you for proposing an elegant vectorised solution for prior specification

and, finnaly, to avoid numerical problems, I constrained a beta parameter of gamma distribution

parameters {
  vector[K_bin] g;     // effects for binary part
  vector[K_cont] b;    // effects for continuous part
  real a[N_re];        // random effect
  real<lower=0> sigma; // standard deviation of random effect

real alpha;  // shape of gamma

}
transformed parameters {
  real<lower=0.001> beta[N];   // scale of gamma
  for(n in 1:N){
    beta[n] = alpha / exp(X_cont[n] * b + a[Groups[n]]);

}
}
model {
  // prior specifications
  // for intercepts
  b[1] ~ cauchy(0, 10);
  g[1] ~ cauchy(0, 10);
  // for other coefs
tail(b, K_cont - 1) ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
if (K_bin > 1) tail(g, K_bin - 1) ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);

// for random effects
  sigma ~ cauchy(0, 25);
  a ~ normal(0, sigma);

// for shape of gamma
  alpha ~ gamma(2, 0.1);  // after Chung et al. 2013

// likelihood contribution
  for (n in 1:N) {

if (Y[n] == 0)
      target += log_inv_logit(X_bin[n] * g);

else
      target += log1m_inv_logit(X_bin[n] * g)

+ gamma_lpdf(Y[n] | alpha, beta[n]);
  }
}


And I probably guessed why the intercept in the binomial part had the "wrong" sign.
In the simulation, I should have been using
W <- rbinom(N, size = 1, prob = (1 - Pi))

On Saturday, 24 December 2016 01:11:35 UTC+3, Michael Betancourt wrote:
I see.  Technically the implementation of the Hurdle Model example is correct
but I would not recommend it given that obfuscates the meaning of the model
and requires some potentially unstable intermediate calculations.  I recommend
implementing the mixture directly, a la

if (y[n] == 0)
  target += log_inv_logit( X_bin[n] * g);
else
  target += log1m_inv_logit(X_bin[n] * g) + gamma_lpdf(y[n] | alpha, beta);

Also, you’ll want an intercept when modeling the logit probability.
 
But that shouldn’t affect your results all that much.  Instead you have some
problems with your prior specifications that are the more likely culprit.

> real<lower=0.001, upper = 100> shape;  // shape of gamma
> …
> shape ~ gamma(0.01, 0.01);

Bad news.  See our recommendations in https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Prior-Choice-Recommendations.


>   for(i in 2:K_cont){
>     b ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
>   }
>   if (K_bin > 1) {
>       for(i in 2:K_bin){
>       g ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
>     }
>   }


You’re missing the index on the b and g here!  Because of the implicit vectorization
you’re actually applying priors to all of the elements of b and g multiple times,
definitely skewing the results.  Either add a “[i]” to the above code or you can do
some cute vector manipulations, such as

tail(b, K_cont - 1) ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);

This will give a warning about Jacobians which you can safely ignore.

>   a ~ normal(0, sigma);

You’ll probably want to try a non-centered parameterization for the random effects.
See the manual for details.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Help to code zero altered gamma glmm
parts:
> On Dec 26, 2016, at 7:07 AM, Marina Varfolomeeva <marina.n...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thank you a lot for your advice, Michael!
>
> As you suggested, I explicitly coded the mixture of two distributions, and changed the prior of the shape parameter
>
> Thank you for proposing an elegant vectorised solution for prior specification
>
> and, finnaly, to avoid numerical problems, I constrained a beta parameter of gamma distribution

Unfortunately, that leads to a Stan program that violates the
fundamental principle of Stan that a model should provide
a finite density for any parameter values meeting the declared constraints.

> parameters {
> vector[K_bin] g; // effects for binary part
> vector[K_cont] b; // effects for continuous part
> real a[N_re]; // random effect
> real<lower=0> sigma; // standard deviation of random effect
> real alpha; // shape of gamma
>
> }
> transformed parameters {
> real<lower=0.001> beta[N]; // scale of gamma
> for(n in 1:N){
> beta[n] = alpha / exp(X_cont[n] * b + a[Groups[n]]);
> }
> }

All that <lower=0.001> will do is reject in the middle of a trajectory
if the constraint gets violated. This degrades model behavior and can even
cause it not to converge at all.

We would instead recommend priors for alpha that avoid zero
(like a lognormal) and priors for a and b that keep the
values from exploding. That will keep beta from being too
low if you have reason to believe it shouldn't be low ahead
of time. The way to express this kind of thing in general is
on the parameters of the model, not on derived quantities.

Now you could actually code up constraints on alpha, b, and a
(based on data X_cont) that would enforce the constraint, but you'd
have to do the transforms manually and include all the Jacobian
adjustments.

- Bob
